sections.title: The customer pays for the battery: what the DTE model is
ps: The Dominion and Duke guides taught how a regulated utility buys through a plan, a certificate and a solicitation, with a {{large-load tariff}} at the end to keep a data center's costs off everyone else's bill. DTE shows a different mechanism, and it is the one that matters most to a storage seller: the data-center customer contracts to pay for utility-owned batteries directly. Under the Oracle agreements the Michigan commission approved in December 2025, DTE Electric will build 1,383 MW of storage — one megawatt for every megawatt the campus contracted — and Oracle's subsidiary pays the full cost over fifteen years while DTE owns the assets in {{rate base}}. The batteries are bought because a customer signed, not because a plan forecast a need.

Three things follow from that design. The purchase orders arrive fast: 332 MW of named projects three months after the order, 660 MW more a month later, 300 MW of third-party tolling three months after that, and a 1.5 GW supply agreement with one manufacturer in between. The load is served from the grid, not from on-site gas — DTE's own words at the announcement were 'existing resources augmented by a new battery storage investment, financed entirely by the project' — so the AI campus becomes a grid customer with a battery portfolio behind it rather than a self-generator. And the argument moves from 'should the utility build this?' to 'who pays and who bears the risk if the campus never fills?', which is the fight now at the Michigan Court of Appeals.

This guide teaches the parts of that mechanism a high-school-STEM reader needs: what a {{special contract}} is and why it is approved differently from a tariff; how a battery is funded by a customer and still owned by a utility; how {{MISO}} counts a battery toward reliability and why a hyperscaler might hand a utility 300 MW of capacity credits for free; the four channels a utility uses to buy storage and what happens when a supplier fails; the credit machinery — triggers, collateral, minimum bills — that stands between one customer's rating and two million other bills; and how the same utility then goes to its regulator for gas plants and a plan that carries the whole thing.

sections.title: Special contract or tariff: two ways to approve one customer
sections.intro: A tariff is a published rate anyone who qualifies can take; a special contract is a negotiated deal for one customer that the commission approves on its own. DTE used the second for its first two data centers and is now writing the first. The rows are the differences that matter to a seller.

sections.title: Ex parte and contested: why the procedure is the politics
ps: **Ex parte.** The commission approves on the utility's filing, without a hearing. The Oracle contracts were approved this way, 3–0, seven weeks after filing and with six conditions attached — a fast answer for a customer that had already paid a $40 million deposit and ordered $2 billion of equipment. The price of speed is a thin record: the Attorney General, who was not heard, petitioned for rehearing, moved to reopen, was denied standing in March 2026 and appealed to the Court of Appeals, where briefs were filed in August. The batteries are being built while the approval that funds them is under review.

**Contested.** For Google, DTE chose a {{contested case}}: testimony, cross-examination, a record. The Attorney General used it to argue for a 90 percent minimum bill instead of 80 and a full-term exit fee. It is slower — the requested decision date, September 10, 2026, passed with no order reported — but an order that survives it is far harder to overturn. The lesson for anyone selling into a special-contract state: the first customer gets speed and a lawsuit, the second gets a hearing and a delay, and the terms that come out of the hearing become the tariff's floor.

**Conditions are the regulator's tariff by other means.** The six conditions on the Oracle order — cost tracking so the customer pays everything, an amended renewable plan, with-and-without-load resource scenarios, emergency procedures that curtail the data center first, six cost-of-service studies in the next rate case, and a general tariff within 90 days — are what a commission writes when it approves a deal it did not design. Each one is a docket a seller can read.

sections.title: Funded by the customer, owned by the utility: the energy storage agreement
ps: In an ordinary {{PPA}} or {{tolling agreement}} a developer owns the battery and the utility pays for its output or its availability. In DTE's energy storage agreement the roles are reversed: DTE owns the battery and the customer pays for it. The 1,383 MW obligation matches the campus's contracted demand one for one — the regulator's way of saying the data center must bring its own capacity to the system — and the customer pays the capital cost over fifteen years while receiving the wholesale market revenues the batteries earn. DTE gets a rate-base asset earning its {{allowed return}}; Oracle gets the accredited capacity its load needs and a hedge on the energy it uses; other customers get, on the commission's condition, none of the bill.

The mechanics are what a storage seller should study. The obligation is filled in tranches, each its own docket: 332 MW of DTE-owned projects (Fish Creek, Cold Creek, Pine River) approved in March 2026 with battery-module supply agreements and {{EPC}} master service agreements whose counterparties are redacted; 660 MW in April (some owned, some tolled); and 300 MW of fifteen-year tolls in July with Key Capture Energy and Copenhagen Infrastructure at a blended $15.30 per kilowatt-month. So a customer-funded obligation is met by self-build *and* by third-party tolls — the developer's battery is paid for by the hyperscaler through the utility. The channel is not exclusive.

The financial reading is about who bears the tail. Fifteen years is shorter than a battery's rate-base life, so the customer pays faster than the asset depreciates; termination payments of up to ten years of minimum charges and collateral that steps up on a downgrade cover the case where the campus stops paying; and the utility's rate case now carries an 'ESA rate base reimbursement' line so that revenue from the customer reduces what other ratepayers fund. When the CFO says the contracts 'make sure that we pay back all of the invested capital, make sure there's no stranded asset risk', this is the machinery he means — and the Court of Appeals is deciding whether it was approved properly.

sections.title: MISO accreditation, and why a hyperscaler hands a utility 300 MW for free
ps: Michigan is in {{MISO}}, a market with a {{capacity market}} that is much thinner than PJM's: most load-serving entities self-supply, and the annual {{planning resource auction}} clears the residual. Each utility must show, for each season, enough accredited capacity — measured in {{zonal resource credit}}s — to cover its share of the reserve requirement. A ZRC is one megawatt of capacity MISO counts on at the hour of need; a 100 MW four-hour battery does not earn 100 ZRCs, it earns what MISO's accreditation method says it will deliver, and from planning year 2028/29 that method becomes 'direct loss of load' — credit based on how much the resource actually helps in the hours the system is short. DTE's 2026 plan models exactly that.

This is why the Google contract contains a line that reads oddly at first: Google supplies DTE with about 300 MW of Zone 7 resource credits at no cost. A new gigawatt of load raises DTE's capacity obligation before the batteries and renewables built for it are accredited; the customer bridging that gap with credits it holds (from its own contracted resources) is the same idea as Duke's letter agreements or WEC's bespoke resources — the load brings capacity with it — expressed in MISO's currency. The December 2025 Oracle order requires DTE's next capacity demonstration to show the data center's effect for the same reason.

The price signal matters less than the accreditation. Zone 7's 2026/27 auction cleared summer at $424/MW-day, down from $667 the year before, after a ten-to-twenty-fold jump the year before that — volatile enough that a utility plans to physical accreditation, not to price. For a storage seller the consequence is that the value of a battery in Michigan is set by MISO's accreditation rules and the utility's demonstration, and a four-hour battery's credit will be discounted as more batteries are added; that is why the 2026 plan reaches for 1.7 GW of long-duration storage — {{compressed-air energy storage}} and {{iron-air}} — from 2037.

sections.title: When the supplier fails: Powin, Trenton Channel and what bankability means to a regulated buyer
ps: **The sequence.** Trenton Channel — 220 MW / 880 MWh at a retired coal site, the largest standalone battery in the Great Lakes — was announced in June 2024 with Powin as supplier. Powin missed deliveries; DTE terminated the contract on May 19, 2025; Powin filed for bankruptcy on June 9. DTE filed a replacement supply agreement with LG Energy Solution Vertech in November 2025 and the commission approved it in April 2026 at more than $30 million less than the original. The plant is due at the end of 2026, roughly on its original schedule.

**What it teaches.** {{Bankability}} to a regulated utility is not only a lender's word. Because the supply agreement itself goes to the commission, a supplier's failure is a regulatory event — a new docket, a new price, a {{prudence review}} question about whether the first choice was reasonable. The utility protected itself with a contract it could terminate and a schedule with slack; the replacement came cheaper because battery prices had fallen and a domestic manufacturer wanted the reference. A seller pitching a utility after this episode is pitching a buyer that has been burned once and whose regulator watched.

**The domestic-content thread.** LG's cells come from Holland, Michigan; the agreement is 'domestic-content-compliant' and DTE's release counts 1,800 LG jobs and 350 construction jobs. Under the {{domestic content bonus}} and the {{FEOC}} rules that fence out certain foreign-owned suppliers from tax-credit-eligible projects, a Michigan-made battery is worth more to a Michigan utility than a cheaper import — and the commission's approval story was written in those terms. DTE never says the word FEOC; it does not need to.

sections.title: From contract to gas plant: the 2026 plan and the certificate of necessity
ps: Michigan's resource plan is a contested case with a 360-day clock, and its distinctive instrument is the {{certificate of necessity}}: a finding, inside the {{IRP}}, that a specific plant is needed and that its cost — up to a cap — may be recovered. DTE's 2026 plan, filed September 24, 2026, asks for two: a ~1,400 MW {{combined cycle}} in Livingston County ($3.9 billion, in service by end-2031) and a ~700 MW combined cycle in Monroe County ($2.5 billion, 2032), both carbon-capture-ready with capture entering service in 2035. It also carries 15 GW of renewables, 4.5 GW of storage including 1.7 GW of long-duration, a 177 MW {{nuclear uprate}} at Fermi 2 by 2036, and the exit from coal in 2032.

The plan's base case is the two signed contracts; a high case carries the full pipeline; an intermediate case sits between. That structure is the CEO's October 2025 remark turned into a filing — 'each additional 1-gigawatt data center could necessitate a new natural gas plant' — and it is the reason the Sierra Club immediately asked for a no-data-center scenario. DTE had turbine down payments and MISO queue positions for the combined cycles by February 2026, so as at Duke the equipment decision precedes the certificate. The OEM is not named.

For the seller the plan's arithmetic is the point: 4.5 GW of storage against 2.1 GW of new gas, where Dominion's plan runs 2 GW of storage against 8.5 GW of gas. A utility whose first data centers brought their own batteries has a plan that leans on storage for the next ones too — and a long-duration line from 2037 that says the four-hour battery's accreditation will not carry the whole load.

items.label: Storage approved by the MPSC in 2026
LG Energy Solution Vertech supply agreement
Tranches explicitly tied to the Oracle obligation in orders

sections.note: The 2022 plan's requirement was 780 MW by 2030; the customer-funded batteries alone meet DTE's share of Michigan's 2,500 MW statewide 2030 target, per the company.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **Reading '1.4 GW of storage' and '332 MW' as a contradiction.** One is the obligation, the other the first tranche of named projects. Both are true; the March 2026 order says so.
**Assuming the LGES deal covers the approved projects.** The arithmetic fits (1,332 + 220 ≈ 1,552 MW) but no document names the eight; the supplier is redacted in the order.
**Treating the Google contract as approved.** The coverage plan assumed it; no order was found through September 25, 2026, and the local tax break was vetoed the same week.

**Forgetting that a special contract's approval can be reversed.** The batteries are under construction while the Court of Appeals reviews the order that funds them; a reversal would not unbuild them but could reopen who pays.

**Pricing to the auction.** Zone 7's capacity price moved $667 → $424 → (earlier) a twenty-fold jump; a battery's value in Michigan is its accreditation under MISO's direct-loss-of-load method, not the clearing price.

cards.q: In DTE's energy storage agreement, who owns the battery and who pays for it?
cards.a: DTE owns it in rate base and earns its allowed return; the data-center customer pays the full capital cost over fifteen years and receives the wholesale revenues. The obligation is one megawatt of storage per contracted megawatt of load.

cards.q: Special contract versus tariff — the one-line difference.
cards.a: A tariff is a published rate any qualifying customer can take; a special contract is a negotiated deal for one customer that the commission approves on its own, with its own conditions.

cards.q: Ex parte versus contested case — what does each buy?
cards.a: Ex parte buys speed (Oracle: seven weeks) at the cost of a thin record that invites appeal; a contested case buys a record that survives appeal at the cost of months (Google: six-plus months and counting).

cards.q: What is a zonal resource credit, and why would Google give DTE 300 MW of them?
cards.a: MISO's unit of accredited capacity, one per megawatt counted on at the hour of need. A new gigawatt of load raises DTE's obligation before the resources built for it are accredited; the customer bridges the gap with credits it holds.

cards.q: Why does a four-hour battery earn fewer capacity credits as more batteries are added?
cards.a: Accreditation measures how much a resource helps in the hours the system is short; once batteries have shifted the shortfall to longer periods, each additional four-hour battery helps less — which is why DTE's plan reaches for long-duration storage from 2037.

cards.q: Name the four channels DTE used to buy storage in 2026.
cards.a: Self-build with a commission-approved supply agreement; build-transfer from a developer; tolling agreements with merchant developers from an RFP; and a framework supply agreement with one manufacturer (LGES, 1.5 GW / 6 GWh).

cards.q: What made the Powin failure a regulatory event rather than just a commercial one?
cards.a: The supply agreement itself is approved by the commission, so replacing the supplier needed a new docket, a new price and a prudence question — DTE's replacement with LGES was approved at more than $30 million less.

cards.q: What is a certificate of necessity?
cards.a: Michigan's version of a CPCN, made inside the IRP: a finding that a specific plant is needed and its cost may be recovered up to a cap. DTE's 2026 plan asks for two, for 1,400 MW and 700 MW of combined cycle.

cards.q: Which of the contract protections did Oracle's July 2026 downgrade test?
cards.a: The collateral with downgrade triggers — DTE says it received additional postings; the minimum bill and termination payment are untouched by a rating change.

cards.q: Why is DTE's storage-to-gas ratio different from Dominion's?
cards.a: Its first customers brought their own batteries under the energy storage agreement, so the 2026 plan runs 4.5 GW of storage against 2.1 GW of new gas; Dominion's plan runs 2 GW of storage against 8.5 GW of gas.

items.q: A commission order says a data center's owner must 'foot the bill' for 1,383 MW of utility-owned storage, and a later order approves 332 MW of named projects. A colleague says the utility cut the battery plan by three-quarters. What is right?
c: The 1,383 MW is the total obligation and the 332 MW is its first tranche of named projects; later orders added 660 MW and 300 MW
The 332 MW is a different customer
items.why: An obligation is filled in tranches, each its own docket.

items.q: Why would a utility choose an ex parte approval for its first hyperscale contract and a contested case for its second?
c: Speed for a customer that had already ordered equipment; then a hearing record for the second so the terms survive appeal — the first choice drew a Court of Appeals challenge
Ex parte is required for contracts over 1 GW
items.why: Procedure is politics: the Oracle order is on appeal, the Google case has a record.

items.q: A supplier misses its delivery dates on a utility-owned battery under a commission-approved supply agreement. What must happen before a replacement can be installed?
c: The utility terminates, negotiates a new supply agreement and files it for commission approval — which is what DTE did with Powin and LGES
The developer takes over the project
The regulator picks a new supplier
items.why: In a regulated self-build the supply agreement is part of the approved project; changing it is a docket.

items.q: A merchant developer wins a 15-year tolling agreement with DTE under the Oracle energy storage agreement. Who ultimately pays for the battery?
c: Oracle, through the utility — the toll is counted against the customer-funded obligation
items.why: The customer-funded obligation is met by tolls as well as self-build, so the hyperscaler pays the developer's battery through the utility.

items.q: Which document in Michigan is where a gas plant's cost cap is set?
c: The certificate of necessity inside the integrated resource plan
items.why: The certificate of necessity is the IRP's finding of need and recoverable cost, up to a cap.

items.q: The MISO Zone 7 capacity price fell 36 percent between two auctions while DTE was buying more batteries than ever. What explains the buying?
c: DTE expected the price to recover
A contract obliges the customer-funded storage, and the utility plans to physical accreditation and its own demonstration, not to the auction price
items.why: Self-supplied utilities plan to accreditation; the price is a residual signal.
